answers.reason: Inclusive or is true when either or both operands are true. Exactly-one xor is false when both operands are true.
The conjunction requires A to be true and B or C to be false. Inclusive B or C is false only when both B and C are false.
not A is false, so (not A) and B is false. A and B is false, so its negation is true.
Material implication is false only for a true antecedent and a false consequent.

answers.reason: A false antecedent makes the material implication true for either value of its consequent. Both assignments to B satisfy the stated information.

The contrapositive of P -> Q is not Q -> not P. Here P is the entire conjunction A and B, so the consequent must be not (A and B). Replacing it by (not A) and (not B) would be stronger and is not equivalent.
De Morgan's law gives not (A or B) = (not A) and (not B). This is true only when both variables are false.
At A=False and B=True, A -> B is true and B -> A is false. That single differing row refutes logical equivalence; the other listed assignments give equal outputs.

answers.answerText: Their outputs agree for every assignment of A and B.
answers.reason: Logical equivalence requires matching outputs on every assignment of the shared variables. Matching names, one matching row, or each having a true row is insufficient.
With A true, a true A -> B requires B true. This is modus ponens; each other listed conclusion contradicts at least one premise.

At A=False and B=True, the implication is true because its antecedent is false, and the second premise B is true, while the conclusion A is false. This is a counterexample to affirming the consequent.

answers.answerText: The argument's form is valid; whether its premises are actually true is a separate question.
answers.reason: The absence of a row with all premises true and conclusion false establishes validity in classical propositional logic. It does not establish actual-world premise truth, an unconditional tautological conclusion, or causation.
